etymologies.etymologyHTML: From earlier randon, from Middle English randoun, raundon, from Old French randon, from randir (“to run, gallop”) (whence French randonnée (“long walk, hike”)), from Frankish *randiju (“a run, race”) or Old Norse rend (“a run, race”), both from Proto-Germanic *randijō, from *rinnaną (“run”, verb), from Proto-Indo-European *(H)r̥-nw- (“to flow, move, run”). Cognate with Middle Low German uprinden (“to jump up”), Danish rende (“to run”). See run.

definitions.definition: A roving motion; course without definite direction; lack of rule or method; chance.

quote.citation: 1648, Robert Herrick, Hesperides, London: H. G. Clarke and Co., published 1844, page 134:
quote.text: Still take advice ; though counsels, when they fly / At random, sometimes hit most happily.

quote.citation: 1815, Sir Walter Scott, The Lord of the Isles, page 216:
quote.text: O ! many a shaft, at random sent, / Finds mark the archer little meant !

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Speed, full speed; impetuosity, force. [14th–17th c.]

quote.citation: 1485, Sir Thomas Malory, chapter X, in Le Morte Darthur, book I:
quote.text: they were messagers vnto kyng Ban & Bors sent from kynge Arthur / therfor said the viij knyghtes ye shalle dye or be prysoners / for we ben knyghtes of kyng Claudas And therwith two of them dressid theire sperys / and Vlfyus and Brastias dressid theire speres and ranne to gyder with grete raundonthey were messengers unto King Ban and Bors sent from King Arthur. Therefore, said the eight knights, ye shall die or be prisoners, for we be knights of King Claudas. And therewith two of them dressed their spears, and Ulfius and Brastias dressed their spears, and ran together with great random.

quote.citation: 1548, Edward Hall, “The triumphant reigne of Kyng Henry the VIII”, in The Union of the two noble and Illustre Famelies of Lancastre and Yorke (Hall’s Chronicle), page 82v:
quote.text: […]  for coragiouſly the two kynges newely foughte with great randon and force, they ſhewed their vigors and ſtrengthes and did ſo nobly that their coũter parties had none aduaũtage.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) The full range of a bullet or other projectile; hence, the angle at which a weapon is tilted to allow the greatest range. [16th–19th c.]

quote.citation: 1624, John Smith, Generall Historie, Kupperman, published 1988, page 144:
quote.text: Fortie yards will they shoot levell, or very neare the marke, and 120 is their best at Random.

quote.citation: 1644, Sir Kenelm Digby, Two Treatises, page 125:
quote.text: […]  the angle at which the miſſive is to mount by ( if we will have it go to its furtheſt randome ) muſt be the half of a right one  […]

definitions.definition: (figuratively, colloquial) An undefined, unknown or unimportant person; a person of no consequence. [from 20th c.]
(printing, historical) A frame for composing type.

quote.text: Utilization of all floor space underneath case racks and randoms is another feature of the modern composing room;  […]

definitions.definition: Occurring for no particular reason; haphazard, unpredictable.
(statistics) Involving an outcome which is impossible to predict, but which may be represented by a probability distribution; in the ideal case, involving outcomes which are equally likely.

quote.citation: July 18 2012, Scott Tobias, AV Club The Dark Knight Rises[1]
quote.text: Where the Joker preys on our fears of random, irrational acts of terror, Bane has an all-consuming, dictatorial agenda that’s more stable and permanent, a New World Order that’s been planned out with the precision of a military coup.

definitions.definition: (computing) Pseudorandom; mimicking the result of random selection.
(informal) Selected for no particular reason; arbitrary; unspecified.
(informal) Being (part of) a varied, unrelated, and apparently arbitrary collection of things; diverse, heterogeneous.
(informal) Apropos of nothing; lacking context, relevance, or any connection to the previous situation; unexpected.
(informal) Of a person: characterized by or often saying random things; habitually using non sequiturs.
(UK, slang) Being out of the ordinary; unusual or unexpected; odd, strange, bizarre.
(intransitive, now uncommon) To wander; to stray; to meander.
